key_facts: Malignant tumour of **epidermal keratinocytes**; the second commonest skin cancer.
Risk factors: cumulative **UV**, older age, fair skin, **AKs**, organ-transplant immunosuppression (65–250× risk), smoking, chronic wounds and scars.
Tender, **keratotic, crusted or ulcerated** nodule on sun-exposed skin that grows over weeks to months.
Can metastasise (about 2–5%): **lip, ear**, large, deep, perineural and immunosuppressed are high risk.
UK (NICE NG12): **suspected cancer (2WW) referral**; surgery is the mainstay.

sections.title: Overview
blocks: A malignant tumour of keratinocytes. It is the second commonest skin cancer, with real potential to metastasise (overall about 2–5%; higher for high-risk tumours). **Lip and ear SCCs metastasise more often** (lip around 10–15% in older series).
Lesions that sit on the UV → keratinocyte dysplasia → SCC pathway, plus clinical forms that conceal SCC.

sub: Rising; about 1 in 4 non-melanoma skin cancers in the UK.
Mostly over 60, more men; outdoor workers.
Organ transplant recipients develop SCCs far more often and more aggressively.
People with chronic lymphocytic leukaemia or HIV.

ul: **Cumulative UV** (outdoor workers, as in [Case 3](condition:basal-cell-carcinoma)), older age, fair skin.
**Immunosuppression:** organ transplant recipients have 65–250× the risk; CLL; HIV.
**Drugs:** azathioprine, voriconazole, hydrochlorothiazide, BRAF inhibitors (vemurafenib monotherapy: KA-type SCCs).
Chronic wounds, scars and burns (**Marjolin ulcer**, ).
Radiation, arsenic, smoking (lip), lichen sclerosus/planus (genital and oral).
Genetic: xeroderma pigmentosum, recessive dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa, albinism.
Path: UV-signature TP53 mutations progress through AK or Bowen's to invasive SCC (see *SCC precursors and related lesions*).

ul: **Cumulative UVB**, sunbeds and PUVA; photosensitising drugs (voriconazole, hydrochlorothiazide).
Precursors: AKs, Bowen's disease (SCC in situ), actinic cheilitis.
**Chronic inflammation and scars**: burns, leg ulcers (Marjolin ulcer), lichen sclerosus, discoid lupus, epidermolysis bullosa.
HPV (especially in immunosuppression and genital/periungual SCC), arsenic, ionising radiation, smoking.
**"It's a wart that won't go"**: a fast-growing, tender keratotic lump on sun-damaged skin needs urgent assessment.

sections.title: Pathophysiology and pathology
blocks: SCC develops step by step from **UV-damaged keratinocytes** that eventually breach the basement membrane.

mech.t: UVB causes **TP53** mutations (UV signature) and then NOTCH and CDKN2A changes.
mech.caption: UVB damages keratinocyte DNA (inset: fused adjacent bases); mutated cells crowd together and begin to invade beneath rough scale.

mech.t: Abnormal cells spread in the epidermis: partial thickness (AK) then full thickness (Bowen's disease, SCC in situ).
Cells break through the basement membrane into the dermis as nests and strands of keratinising cells.
mech.caption: SCC invading through the basement membrane into the dermis, with keratin pearls.

mech.t: Immunosuppression lets mutated clones grow unchecked: why transplant recipients get many aggressive SCCs.
Some tumours invade nerves or spread to regional lymph nodes, especially on high-risk sites.
mech.caption: High-risk sites: lip, ear, temple, scalp and the backs of the hands.

histo: Atypical keratinocytes invading the dermis with **keratin pearls** and intercellular bridges.
Grade (well to poorly differentiated), depth, perineural invasion and margins determine risk and follow-up.

sections.title: Clinical features

ul: An indurated, **tender** keratotic nodule or plaque, or an **ulcer with hard everted edges**, growing over weeks to months, often bleeding.
Sun-exposed sites: scalp, ears, lower lip, the back of the hands, and the lower legs in women.
**Lip SCC:** usually the **lower lip vermilion** (more UV), often on a background of **actinic cheilitis**. Smoking or pipe use. Persistent ulcer or crust, induration.

Variants: well-differentiated/keratinising, cutaneous horn, verrucous carcinoma/carcinoma cuniculatum (plantar, slow, locally destructive; ), keratoacanthoma-type (the [benign lesion](condition:seborrhoeic-keratosis) notes see *Cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (cSCC), including lip SCC*), poorly differentiated, acantholytic, desmoplastic.

blocks: Signs that an AK or Bowen's has become SCC (refer under NG12 1.7.4):

**tenderness/pain**

sub: Annual or more frequent skin surveillance; rapid referral of any new or growing lesion.
SCC is the commonest skin cancer in people with dark skin, often arising in **scars, chronic ulcers or sun-protected sites** and presenting late.

sections.title: Diagnosis and investigations

ul: **Clinical + palpation of regional lymph nodes** (pre-auricular, parotid, cervical, submental/submandibular for the lip; ).
**Biopsy:** excision biopsy is preferred where feasible. Otherwise an incisional/punch biopsy deep enough to assess depth.
**Pathology report items:** differentiation, thickness/depth, perineural and lymphovascular invasion, margins.
**Staging:** the AJCC 8th edition (head and neck cSCC) or UICC 8. The BAD 2020 risk categories (low, high, very high) guide management.
**Imaging** (specialist): ultrasound ± FNA of clinically suspicious nodes; CT/MRI for very high-risk tumours or perineural symptoms. **Consider SLNB only in trials** (not standard UK practice).

blocks: Clinical + dermoscopy (Bowen's: glomerular vessels in clusters + scale). Biopsy if there is doubt or atypia.

blocks: KA, BCC, AK (hypertrophic), Bowen's, irritated SK, viral wart, amelanotic melanoma, Merkel cell carcinoma (rapid red-violet nodule in the elderly), chancre (syphilis; lip), herpes labialis (it heals), aphthous ulcer, traumatic ulcer, and for the lip discoid lupus or lichen planus.
For Bowen's: psoriasis, eczema, superficial BCC, tinea (scrape), and extramammary Paget's (genital).

ul: **NICE NG12 1.7.4:** **consider a suspected cancer pathway referral** (appointment within 2 weeks) for suspected cSCC. [Case 3](condition:basal-cell-carcinoma) (a 6-week indurated bleeding lip ulcer in an outdoor worker) should be referred on that pathway. **Make the referral within 1 working day of deciding.**
**Any lip or oral ulcer that persists for more than 3 weeks** also meets NG12 head-and-neck/oral cancer criteria (suspected cancer pathway or urgent dental referral).
**Do not:** freeze, curette or treat a suspected SCC in primary care unless you are an accredited skin-surgery practitioner working to the IOG.

ul: **Surgery is first-line** (the course answer). Lip: wedge or V-excision ± vermilionectomy for associated actinic cheilitis (maxillofacial/plastics).
Mohs: selected high-risk facial tumours.
**Radiotherapy:** primary treatment if surgery is unsuitable; adjuvant for close/positive margins, perineural invasion or nodal disease.
Nodal disease: neck dissection ± parotidectomy, then adjuvant RT.
Advanced/metastatic: **cemiplimab** (anti-PD-1; NICE TA802, 2022).
**Follow-up:** BAD suggests clinical review for high-risk tumours (e.g. 3–6-monthly for 2 years), plus education about self-examination of the scar and nodes.

**Immunosuppressed/transplant patients:** joint care with the transplant team. Specialists may switch to mTOR inhibitors (sirolimus) or use acitretin chemoprevention. Oral **nicotinamide 500 mg twice daily** reduced new keratinocyte cancers in immunocompetent high-risk patients (ONTRAC 2015), but **showed no benefit in a 2023 trial in transplant recipients**; it is a specialist recommendation.

**Bowen's disease:** treatment is usually a confirmed diagnosis + GP/dermatology plan. An IP may prescribe topical 5-FU 5% **within a documented specialist or GP plan after diagnosis** (e.g. once or twice daily for 3–4 weeks; local protocol).
Actinic cheilitis: refer for diagnosis. Topical options are specialist-initiated (lip reactions can be severe).

blocks.title: Prescribing limits and pitfalls
list: **Don’t**: Freeze, curette or treat suspected SCC in primary care unless accredited.
**5-FU and brivudine**: Never together (fatal DPD inhibition); keep 5-FU off eyes / mucosa.

refer.t: Lip or mouth ulcer > 3 weeks: head-and-neck pathway.
New growth or non-healing area in a long-standing ulcer or scar: biopsy (Marjolin).

sections.title: Red flags and when to refer

ul: Suspected cSCC: **suspected cancer pathway** referral (NICE NG12 1.7.4).
Any lip or mouth ulcer persisting more than 3 weeks: suspected head-and-neck cancer pathway.
A non-healing area or new growth in a long-standing ulcer or scar: biopsy to exclude **SCC (Marjolin ulcer)**.
Local recurrence and tissue destruction.
**Metastasis** to lymph nodes (about 2–5%), higher with high-risk features.
Perineural spread (pain, numbness, cranial nerve palsies).
Most low-risk SCCs are cured by excision.
Five-year survival falls markedly once nodes are involved; high-risk patients need specialist follow-up.

pearls: **Review hydrochlorothiazide** (MHRA) and **voriconazole** (photosensitivity; consider an alternative azole for long-term use in high-risk patients), and remind transplant patients of photoprotection.
Smoking cessation: lip/oral SCC risk and wound healing.
Lip sun protection: an SPF lip balm.
Teach patients to report a new lump in the scar or the neck.
5-FU: expect redness, crusting and soreness. Do not apply near the eyes or mucosa; wash hands after.
Topical 5-FU is minimally absorbed, but **never use it with brivudine** (fatal DPD inhibition), and take care over large areas in patients with known DPD deficiency.
Mark lesions on a body map for follow-up.
